Computing Consumer Tech Space & Aerospace Earnings Menu Money & Markets Economic Indicators Markets Personal Finance Earnings Menu Lifestyle Cars & Bikes Collecting Entertainment Food & Fine Dining Health and Fitness Real Estate Travel General Trivia 15 surprising facts about Election Day that most U.S. voters never learned 
 These 15 surprising Election Day facts cover the Electoral College, voting history and why Americans vote on a Tuesday in November
 1 / 17 List slides 15 surprising facts about Election Day that most U.S. voters never learned List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 21, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Election Day feels like a fixed point on the American calendar — the Tuesday that follows the first Monday in November, every two years for Congress and every four for the presidency. The machinery behind that single date is older and stranger than the routine suggests.
 Congress set the date in 1845 around 19th-century farm schedules, church calendars and market days, not around the commute of an office worker. The candidate with the most votes nationwide does not automatically become president. The U.S. picks its chief executive through the Electoral College, a body of 538 people whose ballots most voters never see cast. Five times, the winner of the national popular vote has lost the presidency.
 The gaps in who gets to vote are just as unusual. Washington, D.C. had no say in presidential elections until the 23rd Amendment took effect in 1961, and the district still has no voting member of Congress. Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens who can help choose a party's nominee in a presidential primary but cannot vote in the November general election — unless they move to one of the 50 states. Women could not vote nationwide until 1920, and the voting age stayed at 21 until 1971.
 These rules decide where campaigns spend money, which states get saturated with advertising and which get skipped, and how a contested result gets resolved. Winner-take-all allocation explains why a handful of competitive states absorb most of the attention while several of the largest states by population see comparatively little. The 12th Amendment explains why a deadlocked Electoral College would be settled by state delegations in the House, with Wyoming carrying the same single vote as California.
 The Election Day facts below cover the origins of the November date, the mechanics of the Electoral College, the long history of voting by mail, the Palm Beach County ballot layout at the center of the 2000 Florida recount, and the time-zone spread that stretches poll closings across roughly six hours. Some are historical curiosities. Others still shape results today.
 Why Election Day falls on a Tuesday 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Congress set Election Day as the Tuesday after the first Monday in November in 1845, and the reasoning was agricultural and religious. Tuesday let rural voters reach a county seat without setting out on a Sunday.
 Most Americans then lived on farms, and the nearest polling place was often the county courthouse. That trip could take a full day by horse or wagon. Sunday was reserved for worship, which ruled out both the journey and the ballot. Monday served as the travel day. Tuesday became the day to vote.
 Wednesday was excluded for a different reason. It was market day in many towns, when farmers hauled goods in to sell, and lawmakers did not want the election colliding with the week's commerce.
 November had its own logic. The fall harvest was mostly in by then, which freed farmers from the fields. The worst winter weather had not yet turned rural roads impassable. A December or January vote risked stranding people in snow. A late-summer date would have conflicted with crops still in the ground.
 The formula itself — the first Tuesday after the first Monday, rather than simply the first Tuesday — exists to keep the election off November 1. That date is All Saints' Day, a Catholic holy day of obligation. It was also when many merchants closed out the previous month's books. Lawmakers preferred not to stack a third obligation onto the same day.
 The 1845 statute governed the choosing of presidential electors. Before it passed, states set their own dates inside a window of several weeks. Voters in some states cast ballots already knowing how neighboring states had gone. Congress extended the same November Tuesday to House elections in 1872, which is why federal races across the country now share a single date.
 The schedule has not moved since. The farm calendar that shaped it stopped governing how most Americans work more than a century ago, but the date it produced still determines when polling places open and close.
 Election Day is not a federal holiday 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Election Day is not one of the 11 federal holidays recognized under U.S. law, so federal offices stay open, mail gets delivered, and most private employers face no national requirement to give staff time off to vote. The federal list runs from New Year's Day through Christmas and includes Juneteenth and Veterans Day. The Tuesday Americans elect their government is absent from it.
 What exists instead is a patchwork. Several states, among them New York, Illinois and Delaware, have made the general election a state holiday. Virginia converted Lee-Jackson Day into an Election Day holiday in 2020. The practical effect varies even in those states — government offices and public schools may close while private businesses operate normally.
 Many states take a narrower approach. They require employers to release workers for a set block of time, often two or three hours, to cast a ballot. Some mandate that the time be paid; others do not. The obligation frequently applies only when an employee's shift does not already leave enough room to reach the polls before they close. Rules also differ on whether advance notice is required and on who picks the hours.
 Congress has weighed a national holiday more than once. The For the People Act, which passed the House in 2019 and again in 2021, would have designated Election Day a legal public holiday for federal workers. The bill never cleared the Senate, and no version of the idea has become law.
 Other democracies schedule around the conflict rather than legislate around it. France, Germany and Brazil hold national elections on Sundays, when most people are already off work. India treats polling day as a paid holiday for eligible voters.
 The U.S. has leaned instead on early voting windows, no-excuse absentee ballots and same-day registration in many states to ease the clash with a workday. Some large employers offer paid time off to vote on their own. Whether a worker gets those hours still depends on the state and the employer.
 The Electoral College decides the president, not the popular vote 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The president is chosen by 538 electors, not by a nationwide vote tally, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. The national popular vote has no formal role in the outcome.
 Each state receives electors equal to its congressional delegation: its House seats plus its two senators. Washington, D.C. holds three electoral votes under the 23rd Amendment, even though it has no voting member of Congress. The two-senator baseline guarantees every state at least three electors. Wyoming, with well under a million residents, holds three, so electoral votes track population only loosely.
 All but two states, along with D.C., use winner-take-all allocation, handing every elector to whoever leads the statewide count, even by a few hundred ballots. Maine and Nebraska are the exceptions. Each awards two electors to the statewide winner and the rest by congressional district, which is why both occasionally split their slates between parties.
 Five presidential elections have ended with the Electoral College winner losing the national popular vote: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000 and 2016. George W. Bush took the presidency in 2000 with 271 electoral votes while Al Gore finished roughly 540,000 votes ahead nationally. In 2016, Donald Trump won the Electoral College while Hillary Clinton led the popular vote by nearly 3 million.
 Winner-take-all also shapes the geography of modern campaigns. Extra votes in a state a candidate already expects to carry add no electors, while flipping a close state by a single ballot delivers its entire bloc. That arithmetic pushes money, candidate travel and advertising toward a short list of competitive states, including Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Georgia, depending on the cycle.
 Electors meet in their state capitals in December and cast separate ballots for president and vice president. Congress counts those ballots in a joint session in early January. The November vote Americans think of as choosing a president is technically a vote for a slate of electors pledged to that candidate.
 Inauguration Day used to be in March 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Presidents were sworn in on March 4 for most of American history, about four months after the November election. The 20th Amendment, ratified in 1933, moved the start of a presidential term to January 20 and cut the wait between Election Day and the transfer of power by roughly six weeks.
 The March date reflected the logistics of the late 18th century. Each state counted ballots by hand. Results then traveled to the capital, the winner was formally notified, and a new administration had to be assembled and moved to Washington. A long runway made sense when the trip from Georgia or Massachusetts could take weeks on horseback or by ship.
 Railroads, the telegraph and the telephone erased the need for that cushion. The transition from Herbert Hoover to Franklin D. Roosevelt over the winter of 1932 and 1933 showed the cost of keeping it. The Great Depression had reached its worst point. Banks were failing and unemployment kept climbing. For four months, a defeated president and a president-elect with no legal authority occupied the same stage.
 Congress had already approved the amendment and sent it to the states in 1932. Ratification came in January 1933 — too late to apply to Roosevelt's own first swearing-in. That ceremony took place on March 4, 1933, the last March inauguration in U.S. history.
 The measure is often called the lame duck amendment because it did more than move Inauguration Day. It also shifted the start of congressional terms from March to January 3. That shortened the stretch in which lawmakers who had already lost reelection kept writing laws. It also ended a system under which a newly elected Congress did not convene until 13 months after voters chose it.
 Every president since Roosevelt's second term began in 1937 has taken office on January 20. When that date falls on a Sunday, the oath is administered privately and the public ceremony follows the next day. That happened for Dwight Eisenhower in 1957, Ronald Reagan in 1985 and Barack Obama in 2013.
 Faithless electors can vote against their state's results 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A presidential elector who votes for someone other than the candidate who carried their state is called a faithless elector, and it has happened more than 150 times in American history. No such vote has ever changed the outcome of a presidential election.
 The rules governing electors vary from state to state. Some states require by law that an elector back the winner of their state's popular vote, and those laws can impose a fine, void the deviant ballot, or remove and replace the elector. Other states set no binding requirement at all, leaving electors free to vote as they choose once the Electoral College convenes in December.
 The Supreme Court settled the central legal question in 2020. In Chiafalo v. Washington, the justices ruled unanimously that a state may require its electors to support the candidate who won that state and may penalize or replace those who refuse. The ruling confirmed state authority over electors without abolishing the position, and it changed nothing in states that never passed binding laws.
 The 2016 election produced seven faithless presidential votes, the most since 1872. Three electors in Washington state backed Colin Powell instead of Hillary Clinton. One Texas elector voted for Ron Paul rather than Donald Trump. Each of those ballots appeared in the official certificates sent to Congress.
 Earlier cases tended to be lone acts — a protest, a tribute to a deceased figure, or a nod to a regional candidate — with no realistic path to altering the result. Electoral College margins have usually been wide enough that scattered defections carried no mathematical weight.
 What the practice illustrates is that the Electoral College is a vote cast by people, not an automatic tally generated by the November returns. Electors are selected by state parties, gather in December in their state capitals, and sign physical certificates that a joint session of Congress counts the following January.
 Ties go to the House of Representatives 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A presidential election that produces no 270-vote majority in the Electoral College is decided by the House of Representatives under the 12th Amendment. The House does not vote the way it does on ordinary legislation. Each state delegation casts a single vote, so 26 states — not 218 members — are needed to pick a president.
 The House chooses from among the three candidates with the most electoral votes. A quorum for that purpose requires at least one member from two-thirds of the states. Delaware, with its single House member, controls the same one vote as California's delegation of more than 50. A delegation that splits evenly casts no vote at all, so an internally divided state effectively abstains.
 This procedure, known as a contingent election, has produced a president twice. In 1800, Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr finished tied in the electoral count, and the House needed 36 ballots to settle on Jefferson. That deadlock exposed a flaw in the original rules. It led directly to the 12th Amendment, ratified in 1804, which separated the balloting for president from the balloting for vice president.
 The 1824 contest became the first contingent election held under those revised rules. Four candidates split the electoral vote, and none reached a majority. The House chose John Quincy Adams, even though Andrew Jackson had won more popular votes and more electoral votes than any other candidate. Jackson's supporters called the result a corrupt bargain, and he won the rematch in 1828.
 The vice presidency follows a separate path. If no vice-presidential candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, the Senate decides between the top two finishers. Each senator casts an individual ballot rather than voting by state. That has happened once, in 1837, when the Senate elected Richard Mentor Johnson.
 No contingent election has occurred since 1824, but the mechanism remains available any time a third-party or independent candidate wins enough electors to block a majority. Under the 20th Amendment, if the House has not chosen a president by Inauguration Day, the vice president-elect acts as president until it does.
 D.C. only gained electoral votes in 1961 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Residents of Washington, D.C. could not vote for president until the 23rd Amendment was ratified in 1961, about 160 years after the federal government moved to the district. The amendment granted the capital electors but capped the total at the number held by the least populous state — three in practice.
 The district cast its first presidential ballots in 1964 and awarded its three electoral votes to Lyndon B. Johnson. Every Democratic nominee since has carried it, and no Republican nominee ever has.
 The cap is the unusual piece of the arrangement. A state receives electors in proportion to its House seats plus its two Senate seats. D.C. is held below that formula no matter how many people live there. More than 670,000 people live in the district, a larger population than Wyoming's or Vermont's. Each of those states also holds three electoral votes, and each also seats two U.S. senators.
 Representation stops at the presidency. The district elects a delegate to the House of Representatives who sits on committees, files bills and votes in committee. That delegate cannot vote when the full House decides whether a bill passes. D.C. has no senators at all. Residents pay federal income tax and serve in the armed forces without a voting voice in the body that writes federal law. That grievance is the source of the "taxation without representation" slogan printed on district license plates.
 Local self-government arrived later still. Congress ran the city directly for most of its history, until the District of Columbia Home Rule Act of 1973 created an elected mayor and council. Walter Washington took office in 1975 as the first elected mayor in more than a century. Congress still reviews local legislation and can block it, and it has used that power.
 Statehood is the proposed remedy. The House passed bills to admit the district as a state in 2020 and again in 2021, and both died in the Senate. Opponents argue the Constitution requires the seat of government to sit outside any state, and that changing D.C.'s status would take a constitutional amendment rather than an ordinary law.
 Puerto Rico residents can't vote for president 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens by birth, but those living on the island cannot cast a ballot for president in the November general election. The same exclusion applies to residents of Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.
 The reason is structural, not a matter of citizenship status. Puerto Rico has been under U.S. sovereignty since 1898, and its residents received U.S. citizenship through the Jones-Shafroth Act of 1917. The Constitution assigns presidential electors to states, and the 23rd Amendment named Washington, D.C. as the single exception to that rule. Territories appear in neither arrangement, so Puerto Rico has no electoral votes to award and no mechanism for island ballots to count toward the 270 needed to win.
 The exclusion covers the general election only. Both major parties hold presidential nominating contests on the island, so residents help choose who appears on the November ballot in the 50 states. A voter in San Juan can help pick a nominee and then have no say in whether that nominee reaches the White House.
 Residency, not citizenship, decides the question. A Puerto Rican who moves to Florida, New York or any other state can vote for president as soon as that state's residency and registration requirements are met. The person's legal status does not change — the address does. Millions of people of Puerto Rican heritage live in the mainland U.S., which is why both parties campaign for Puerto Rican voters in states such as Florida and Pennsylvania.
 Congressional representation is limited in a similar way. Puerto Rico elects a Resident Commissioner to the House of Representatives, who serves a four-year term, sits on committees and speaks in debate but cannot vote on final passage of legislation. The island has no senators.
 The territory's political status remains unsettled. Statehood, independence and continued commonwealth arrangements have each been put to island voters in a series of nonbinding referendums. The results have varied, and none has produced action from Congress, which holds the authority to change the status.
 Mail voting dates back to the Civil War 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Voting by mail is not a 21st-century invention. Its American origins run to the Civil War, when Union states passed laws letting soldiers in the field cast ballots away from their home precincts instead of forfeiting the vote while in uniform.
 Pennsylvania and Wisconsin were among the states that enacted soldier voting measures during the 1860s. Methods differed from place to place. Some states gathered ballots at army camps and shipped them back to be counted at home. Others allowed a soldier to name a proxy in his home district to cast a vote on his behalf. By the 1864 presidential election, most Union states had set up some way for troops to take part.
 Civilian access widened slowly over the decades that followed. States wrote absentee provisions for voters traveling on business, voters physically unable to reach a polling place and voters living far from the precinct where they were registered. Eligibility stayed narrow for a long time, and a voter usually had to state a specific excuse to qualify.
 Both world wars pushed the system further. With millions of Americans stationed overseas, Congress and the states built procedures to send ballots abroad and return them in time to be counted. That patchwork was standardized by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act of 1986. The law guarantees absentee voting rights to military personnel, their families and U.S. citizens living outside the country.
 Oregon became the first state to run every election by mail. Voters there approved a ballot measure in 1998 requiring it, and the system was fully in place by 2000. Washington state and Colorado later moved to all-mail elections of their own.
 The 2020 election produced the largest single-cycle expansion. Many states relaxed excuse requirements or sent ballots and applications to more voters during the COVID-19 pandemic. Mail ballots accounted for a much larger share of the total than in any previous presidential year. The scale was new. The method was more than 150 years old.
 Women couldn't vote nationally until 1920 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 19th Amendment, ratified on August 18, 1920, barred states from denying the vote on the basis of sex. It arrived more than 70 years after the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 put women's suffrage on the national agenda.
 What the amendment did not do was deliver the ballot to every woman in practice.
 Several Western states and territories moved first. Wyoming Territory granted women the vote in 1869 and kept that provision when it joined the Union in 1890, making Wyoming the first state where women could vote. Colorado, Utah and Idaho also extended suffrage to women before the federal amendment passed. By the 1910s, a woman's ability to cast a ballot depended largely on which side of a state line she lived on.
 Ratification changed the constitutional text without dismantling the machinery states used to screen voters. Poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation at registration offices continued to block Black women across the South for decades. The amendment prohibited sex-based exclusion. It said nothing about the requirements that were race-neutral on paper and that Southern states had built to keep Black residents off the rolls.
 The Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed literacy tests and authorized federal oversight of voter registration in jurisdictions with records of discrimination. For Black women in much of the South, that law — not the 19th Amendment — marked the point when voting became reliably accessible. That is a gap of 45 years between the constitutional guarantee and its practical reach.
 Native American women faced a separate barrier. Many Native Americans were not recognized as U.S. citizens until the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924, four years after the 19th Amendment took effect. Even then, several states used residency rules, guardianship claims and tax-status arguments to keep Native residents from registering. Arizona and New Mexico maintained restrictions on Native voting until 1948, when court rulings in both states struck those restrictions down.
 The voting age dropped to 18 in 1971 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 26th Amendment lowered the national voting age from 21 to 18 in 1971, and it moved through the states faster than any other amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Congress approved it in March of that year, and the states finished ratifying it in July — a span of roughly three months.
 Vietnam drove the argument. Men were drafted and sent to fight at 18 with no say in electing the officials who set that policy. "Old enough to fight, old enough to vote" became the campaign's shorthand, though the idea dated to World War II, when the draft age was lowered to 18.
 Georgia moved first among the states, lowering its own voting age to 18 in 1943. Kentucky followed in the 1950s. Alaska joined the union in 1959 with a voting age of 19, and Hawaii with one of 20. Those states were exceptions. Most held at 21 until the amendment made the rule uniform.
 The direct trigger was a court ruling. Congress had tried to lower the voting age by statute in the 1970 extension of the Voting Rights Act. In Oregon v. Mitchell, the Supreme Court upheld that provision for federal elections but struck it down as applied to state and local contests.
 The split decision left election officials facing two sets of voter rolls — one listing 18-year-olds eligible to vote for president and Congress, another barring them from races for governor, mayor and the state legislature. The cost and administrative work of running parallel registration systems pushed lawmakers toward a constitutional fix instead.
 Ratification arrived in time for 18-year-olds to vote in the 1972 presidential election. The amendment borrowed its structure from earlier voting rights amendments, barring denial or abridgment of the vote "on account of age" for citizens 18 or older. That age remains the floor nationwide, and no state may set a higher minimum for federal elections.
 The 2000 butterfly ballot changed how states design ballots 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Palm Beach County, Florida ran a punch-card ballot in the 2000 presidential election with candidate names printed down both sides of one center column of punch holes. Thousands of voters reported that the layout led them to mark the wrong candidate.
 The problem sat in the alignment. Al Gore's name was listed second in the left column, but his punch hole was the third one down. Pat Buchanan's name ran across from Gore's on the right side, beside the second hole. A voter reading down the left column and punching the second hole recorded a vote for Buchanan.
 Buchanan took roughly 3,400 votes in Palm Beach County. That total ran far above his results in comparable Florida counties and above his showing across the state. The county leans heavily Democratic and has a large retiree population. Buchanan said publicly that he doubted most of those votes were meant for him.
 The statewide margin made the layout consequential. George W. Bush was certified the winner of Florida by 537 votes, which delivered the state's electoral votes and the presidency. The number of disputed ballots in that one county ran several times larger than the margin.
 Punch-card equipment created a second problem across Florida. Machines left chads — the small rectangles meant to be punched clear of the card — partly attached, so voter intent became a judgment call. Canvassing boards inspected cards by hand for days until the U.S. Supreme Court halted the recount in Bush v. Gore.
 Congress passed the Help America Vote Act in 2002. The law sent federal money to states to retire punch-card and mechanical lever machines in favor of optical-scan and electronic systems. It also created the Election Assistance Commission, required statewide voter registration databases and established provisional ballots for voters whose eligibility is questioned at the polls.
 The Election Assistance Commission has since published ballot design guidance for election offices. It covers plain-language instructions, typography and consistent alignment between a candidate's name and the space a voter uses to mark it.
 Early media calls have gotten elections wrong before 
 Illustration: Quartz
 News organizations have projected the wrong winner on election night more than once, and the best-known case is the Chicago Tribune's "Dewey Defeats Truman" front page from 1948. Harry Truman won that election, and a photograph of him holding up the mistaken edition became a lasting image in American politics.
 The Tribune's error grew out of a compressed printing schedule and pre-election polling that pointed consistently toward New York Governor Thomas Dewey. The paper went to press before the returns settled. Truman took 303 electoral votes to Dewey's 189, with Strom Thurmond winning 39.
 Election night 2000 produced a messier version of the same failure, with far more at stake. Television networks called Florida for Al Gore early in the evening on the strength of exit polling, then withdrew the call as actual returns came in. Around 2 a.m., they gave the state to George W. Bush. That projection was pulled back as well once the margin narrowed. Florida was not resolved for more than a month, ending with the Supreme Court's decision in Bush v. Gore.
 Both failures trace back to the same problem: projections built on samples and partial counts rather than finished tallies. Exit polls can skew when some voters are more willing to answer a pollster than others. Early returns can mislead when they arrive from parts of a state that do not reflect the whole. Mail and absentee ballots add another layer, because many states count them after in-person votes, which can shift an apparent lead hours or days after polls close.
 The fallout changed how projections get made. Voter News Service, the consortium that supplied network exit poll data in 2000, was disbanded in 2003. Edison Research has run the network exit poll since 2004, and the Associated Press built a separate survey, AP VoteCast, alongside its own vote count.
 Decision desks now weigh actual returns, absentee counts and statistical models against one another before declaring a winner. Close races that once drew a confident midnight call can now sit uncalled for days.
 Poll closing times can span six hours across the country 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Polls do not close at the same hour nationwide. Roughly six hours separate the first precincts to shut from the last, because the 50 states sit across six time zones and each state writes its own rules on voting hours.
 Parts of Indiana and Kentucky close at 6 p.m. local time in the Eastern zone, which puts their returns among the first to appear on election night. Alaska and Hawaii sit at the other end of the schedule. Voters there are still casting ballots around midnight Eastern time, long after counting has begun on the East Coast.
 Geography explains only half of the gap. Poll hours come from state statutes, so two neighboring states in the same time zone can stop voting an hour apart. Some close at 7 p.m. local time, others at 8 p.m., and a few later than that. Most states also allow anyone already standing in line when the doors shut to cast a ballot, which pushes the final votes past the posted hour.
 The staggered close produced one of the longest-running disputes in election coverage. In 1980, NBC projected Ronald Reagan the winner early in the evening, and Jimmy Carter conceded while West Coast polls were still open. Congress later held hearings on whether early projections discourage Western voters from turning out. The question was never settled, but the episode reshaped newsroom practice, and television networks now hold a state's projection until that state's polls have closed.
 The clock spread also shapes how election night unfolds. Early tallies from the Atlantic seaboard can point one direction, then shift as Central, Mountain and Pacific counts arrive, even when the eventual winner never changes. States that close early and count quickly tend to report well before states that close later or process large volumes of mail ballots.
 A single national contest run across a continent-sized country is really dozens of separate state elections ending at different moments. The count arrives in waves.
 Primary elections and Election Day are not the same thing 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Election Day refers to the general election held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, when voters choose who takes office. Primaries and caucuses, Super Tuesday included, come months earlier and decide only which candidates appear on that November ballot.
 Super Tuesday has no fixed date on the calendar. It lands in early March of a presidential election year and marks the point when the largest group of states holds nominating contests on the same day. The lineup shifts from cycle to cycle. State legislatures and state parties set their own primary dates, so a state that votes on Super Tuesday one year may move earlier or later the next.
 Rules about who may take part vary by state. An open primary lets any registered voter request either party's ballot, whatever their own registration says. A closed primary limits participation to voters registered with that party, which leaves independents in those states without a voice in picking nominees. Semi-closed systems sit in between, allowing unaffiliated voters to choose a party ballot at the polling place.
 Caucuses run on different mechanics altogether. Rather than marking a private ballot and leaving, participants meet in person at an appointed hour in school gyms, community centers and similar rooms. They back a candidate in the open, sometimes by moving into groups around the room. Discussion and several rounds of realignment can follow before anyone tallies a result. Iowa's caucuses have long been among the first nominating contests of the cycle, which gives a small state substantial influence over which candidates survive the early months.
 The full calendar stretches across most of an election year. Nominating contests run from January into June, the parties hold conventions over the summer to confirm their nominees, and the general election campaign fills the final stretch before November. Turnout in primaries runs lower than turnout in the November general election. The field most voters see on Election Day was narrowed by a smaller slice of the electorate.
